title: No Verified Incident Can Excuse an Unregulated Dog Trade
excerpt: Claims about stolen pets, poison, and rabies require documented sources. Verified health guidance still demands urgent reform, quarantine, and abolition by 2030.
body_html:
Every stolen companion matters. Every rabies exposure matters. But public anger must rest on facts that can be checked: named cases, dates, locations, seizure records, court judgments, and health alerts. Available reporting does not establish a verified incident supporting claims about cyanide bait, a pet-theft conviction, or uninspected dog-meat contamination. Those claims must not be presented as fact.

Myths cannot replace evidence

“Tradition” does not excuse theft, illegal transport, cruelty, or quarantine breaches. “Farm-raised dogs” cannot erase the need for traceability, vaccination records, lawful transport, veterinary inspection, and transparent slaughter controls. But no responsible investigation can claim that no dog farms exist without documented supply-chain audits. It can demand proof from operators and authorities.

Public health still demands hard safeguards

Rabies spreads when infected saliva enters through bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. After possible exposure, wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical assessment. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. World Health Organization guidance supports immediate care before symptoms develop.

Demand proof. Demand protection.

Vietnamese families, pet owners, veterinarians, and local leaders can demand records, quarantine enforcement, traceable transport, and prosecution of documented crimes. Household rabies incidents and commercial supply-chain risks are parallel biosecurity concerns; neither should be falsely presented as proof of the other.

State health targets are not the same as SDE’s campaign demand. SDE calls for complete abolition of the dog-meat trade by 2030. Sign the national petition. Add your name to a public demand for action, then follow campaign updates reaching decision-makers.

A stolen companion deserves more than an unverified headline. Families deserve more than rumors about poison, raids, or disease. They deserve records, enforcement, and honest public-health communication.

Available reporting does not verify the dramatic incidents often used to defend claims about Vietnam’s dog-meat supply chain. That failure demands evidence—not invented scenes or unsupported conclusions. Authorities and operators should disclose transport records, quarantine controls, veterinary inspection, and court documents where crimes occurred.

Rabies remains unforgiving. Infected saliva can enter through bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. After possible exposure, wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical care for post-exposure prophylaxis. Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route.

Vietnamese families, pet owners, veterinarians, and community leaders can demand transparent enforcement. Household exposures and commercial trade risks are separate questions, but both require protection. SDE calls for complete abolition by 2030.
